newsitem.title: USA: Fitch says cuts Pittsburgh, Pa., GOs to BBB-plus.
newsitem.headline: Fitch says cuts Pittsburgh, Pa., GOs to BBB-plus.

text.p: The underlying rating on Pittsburgh's general obligation bonds is lowered to 'BBB+' from 'A-' by Fitch Investors Service.
The rating action reflects continuing structural imbalance in financial operations, the risks attendant upon the proposal to delay obtaining balance until 1998 and the city's heavy debt level.
The general fund's accumulated deficit peaked at $37.3 million in 1994.
Under the March 1995 agreement, the Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority (PWSA) will pay the city $95 million over three years for certain assets transferred to the authority.
The city is using these moneys to fund the accumulated deficit, as well as to provide the general fund some operating revenues through 1997 as it bridges its structural gap.
The city used the initial $35 million of these funds and other payments from PWSA to reduce the accumulated deficit to $15.3 million in 1995.
All source tax revenues have remained relatively static since 1990 -- assessed valuation continues to fluctuate and is now below the 1990 level.

Non-recurring revenues continue to be used for recurring costs. The city was unsuccessful in balancing its 1994 budget through expenditure reductions. While additional expenditure reductions were subsequently made, the 1995 and 1996 budgets continued to include non- recurring revenues.

Officials report that $16.1 million (4.2%) of 1996's $313.8 million budget is funded through non-recurring sources. In early October, the Competitive Pittsburgh Task Force released its recommendations for closing the annual structural deficit.

The recommendations, which range from instituting fees for residential garbage collection to making substantial changes in labor operations, appear to carry substantial risks as to implementation for the 1998 budget. The outlook remains negative.

The upcoming sale of bonds to fund a portion of the unfunded pension liability is considered to be credit neutral as the increased debt issuance largely addresses what was a significant negative credit factor -- a large unfunded pension liability accompanied by escalating and non-deferrable pension funding requirements.
While the pension fund was never intended to be debt funded, the issuance levels the funding requirements without taking up- front budget savings.
